en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuance of Ximing Monastery.
Chapter Five: On Protecting the State.
Regarding the explanation of this chapter, there are briefly two points: first, the explanation of the chapter title; second, the formal explanation of the text.
Regarding the explanation of the title of this chapter: according to the *Benji* (Original Record), there are two types of lands:
first, the mundane, which consists of those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary worldlings;
second, the supramundane, ranging from the ten levels of faith up to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
There are two kinds of thieves:
first, external ones, such as robbers and predators;
second, internal ones, namely the afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are two kinds of protection:
first, the external, which consists of the hundred classes of spirits;
second, the internal, which is wisdom.
Whether internal or external, all are the spiritual powers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Now, the explanation is as follows:
because Prajñāpāramitā can protect the realms of humans and devas, it is called "Protecting the State" (Huguo).
Sūtra: "At that time... up to the Prajñāpāramitā.
Commentary:
From here on is the second section: the formal explanation according to the text.
That which can protect the fruit of Buddhahood and the practices of the ten stages constitutes internal protection (*adhyātma-rakṣā*).
Protecting the realms of humans and devas constitutes external protection (*bahirdhā-rakṣā*).
Having already explained the two kinds of internal protection above, the second section now elucidates the "Chapter on Protecting the State.
According to the *Benji* (Original Record), this is divided into four parts:
first, the practice of the Dharma; second, the capacity for protection; third, the citation of scriptural evidence; and fourth, the attainment of benefits.
There are three aspects to the practice of the Dharma:
first, the admonition to listen; second, the exhortation to uphold; and third, the explanation of protection.
This [present case] corresponds to the first two, as can be known from the sutra.
Now, the explanation is as follows: it is not so.
Within a single category, there are three distinct textual sections.

First, the imperial decree permits and encourages the upholding [of the Dharma]; next, from "In that land" onwards, there is a detailed explanation of protecting the Dharma; finally, from "At that time, Śākyamuni" onwards, the benefits obtained by the assembly are distinguished.
This is the first [section].
The exhortation to listen, the permission to speak, and the encouragement to uphold [the teaching] may be understood from the sutra.
The sutra states:
"When the land reaches the point of national collapse.
The commentary states:
This is the second section from here on, providing a detailed explanation of the protection of the Dharma.
Within this, there are three parts:

first, an extensive explanation of the protection of the Dharma; second, from "Great King, in the past... onwards, citing the ancients to corroborate the present; and third, from "Great King, at sixteen years of age... onwards, concluding with an exhortation to uphold [the teaching].
Within the extensive explanation, it is further divided into three parts:

first, the explanation of protecting the state; second, from "Great King, not only... onwards, the explanation of protecting merit; and third, from "Great King, not only... onwards, the explanation of protecting against various calamities.
Regarding the protection of the kingdom, there are four distinct sections:

first, clarifying the time of protection; second, explaining the method of protection; third, from "Your kingdom" onwards, clarifying the essence of the protector; and fourth, from "Great King" onwards, manifesting the difficulty of that which is protected.
This is the first clarification regarding the protection of time.

In reality, the protection of the state's way pertains to all times; however, to highlight the essential times, the protection of the Dharma is explained by citing such events as the conflagration at the end of an eon.
Regarding the term "kalpa-conflagration" (劫燒), it is called a kalpa-conflagration because it destroys the kingdom; it does not refer to the great fire calamity among the three calamities.
The Sūtra states:
"One should invite one hundred Buddhas and [visualize] one hundred arhats."
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the second section, which explains the alternative interpretation of Dharmapāla.
Within this, there are three parts:
First, the field of merit is requested; second, the offering is clarified; and lastly, the time for the discourse is manifested.
Within the section on the field of merit, there are three distinct parts:
first, the field of merit consisting of the various sages; second, the assembly of listeners at the lecture hall; and third, the request for the teacher to deliver the discourse.
This is the first point.
It means that because the actual bodies of the Three Honored Ones above are difficult to assemble, one establishes a hundred images so as to provide a complete field of merit for future generations.
The Sūtra says:
"From a community of one hundred bhikṣus up to the seven assemblies all listen together.
The commentary states:
"The second refers to the audience at the lecture assembly."
There are three [assemblies]: first, the assembly of one hundred bhikṣus; second, the assembly of four hundred great multitudes; third, the assembly of seven groups.
Regarding the "one hundred bhikṣus," some say:
Before each seat there were one hundred bhikṣus.
If that were so, there would be ten thousand people; with such a multitude, the Dharma discourse could not be completed.
As for the mention of "one hundred" here, it means that before each seat there was one bhikṣu who supervised the assembly; thus, they are said to be "one hundred."
Regarding the "fourfold assembly," this refers to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Some say that śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās are excluded.
Now it is said:
they are included within the assemblies of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding the "seven assemblies," these refer to the three assemblies such as the śrāmaṇeras that follow upon the aforementioned four assemblies.
The seven assemblies are the assemblies of those who come and go.
Question:
Each seat has six categories, and each [of those] has one hundred categories; what is the meaning of this?
The commentary says:
This is because he wishes to adorn the assembly for the preaching of the Dharma.
Question:
Since the fourfold assembly already includes the bhikṣus, why is it necessary to mention "one hundred bhikṣus" separately?
It is said to be "one hundred" in order to demonstrate that within each assembly, there must necessarily be one person serving as the presiding elder (upādhyāya).
Question: What is the distinction between the "great assembly" (mahāsannipāta) and the seven groups of followers? Some say:
They are spoken of as distinct categories for the sake of classification, yet they are not necessarily distinct in substance.
Alternatively, it may be that all four great assemblies are themselves the assembly of the Mahāyāna.
As for the mention of the "seven assemblies," these refer to the assembly of the Śrāvakas.
Sūtra: He invited one hundred Dharma masters to lecture on the Prajñāpāramitā.
Commentary:
Third, requesting the teacher to expound the sutra:
from "The Hundred Lions" up to "Making Offerings to the Triple Gem."
The commentary states:
Third, the explanation of the method of making offerings.
There are three major categories:
First, it clarifies the three types of offerings made to the Triple Gem, namely lamps, incense, and flowers.
Regarding the phrase "a hundred lamps" and so forth, this means that before each seat there is one lamp, one flower, and one incense stick.
If it were not so, it would result in ten thousand flowers, which is difficult to accomplish.
The Sūtra states:
"One should provide the three robes and requisites as an offering to the Dharma Master."
The commentary states:
Second, the method for making special offerings to the Dharma Master.
Regarding the term "requisites" (pariṣkāra), there are two interpretations.
According to one tradition, the ten items are as follows:
first, the three robes; second, the alms bowl; third, the sitting mat; fourth, the razor; fifth, the small knife; sixth, the water filter; seventh, the bowl bag; eighth, the needle case.
The *Jing sanzang* (淨三藏) states:
"Regarding the 'three robes and ten articles,' this is likely an error by the translator who separated them into two distinct sections.
Not relying on the Sanskrit original, he separately discussed the three robes and divided the ten articles; his interpretation of *li* (離) as 'separation' is a most reckless conjecture."
The thirteen requisites provide benefit for those of middle and inferior capacities.

Regarding these thirteen requisites: first, the *saṃghāṭī*; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*; third, the *antarvāsa*; fourth, the *nivāsana*; fifth, the *upānaha* (skirt); sixth, the *upānaha-parivāra* (secondary skirt); seventh, the *saṃkakṣikā* (breast-cloth); eighth, the *pratisaṃkakṣikā* (secondary breast-cloth); ninth, the *varṣāśāṭī* (rain-cloak); tenth, the *kāyaprocchanī* (body-wiping cloth); eleventh, the *mukhaprocchanī* (face-wiping cloth); twelfth, the *keśapratigrahaṇa* (hair-receiving cloth, worn during shaving to prevent hair from falling on the ground); and thirteenth, the *gaṇḍūṣapratigrahaṇa* (wound-covering cloth).

The summary verse says: "The three robes together with the sitting mat; the lower garment and the two types of upper robes come in pairs; the rain-cloak, the towel for wiping the body and face, the shaving tool, and the covering for sores.

Although there are two interpretations, this still does not clarify whether the "several tens and hundreds" mentioned in the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Renyōkyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) refers to the number ten or the character *shi* (ten).
Sūtra: He eats his midday meal in moderation and likewise observes the proper timing.
The commentary states:
Third, the method for making offerings of food to the Dharma Master, or alternatively, providing offerings to the entire assembly.
The Sūtra says:
The Great King preaches this sutra twice a day; some versions read "preaches and recites this sutra.
The commentary states:
This is the third section, concerning the time for preaching the sutra.
One must exert one's full energy in lecturing; therefore, it follows the two meals, and the lecture likewise occurs at both times.
The Sūtra says:
"In your land... until protecting your land."
The commentary states:
Third, it clarifies their capacity for protection.
Regarding the hundred classes of deities, according to the *Mūla-ṭīkā*, they derive from the interpretation of the Rishi Suvarṇākṣa.
This immortal leads the ghosts and spirits; fundamentally there are ten locations, which expand into one hundred.
As for the ten: first is the Great Deity, who is able to transform all other deities.
The two divine youths were sons of Maheśvara; they entered the hermitage at night.
According to the laws of the seers, small children are not to be killed. The seer prophesied that when they reached the age of sixteen, they would become great seers and then inevitably die.
Since his words were not empty, this could not be avoided.
Maheśvara then detained this boy at the perpetual age of fourteen; taking young children as his followers, he thus harmed the infants of the world.
If he were fifteen years old, this boy would no longer cause harm.
The third is the Mother Goddess, who is the wet-nurse of the Youth (Kumāra).
The fourth is the Brahma-god Maheśvara, who has three eyes on his face and possesses all-encompassing wisdom.

If one loses an object and cannot find it, he casts a spell upon the child’s face so that a fourth eye grows there; the owner then goes directly to retrieve the object, and once he has obtained it, the eye returns to being lost.
The five household deities obstruct all vows, causing both good and evil undertakings to fail.
The six dragon deities are characterized by much greed and anger.
The seven asura deities are able to bind and strike down humans, devas, and others.
Furthermore, there are two types of warriors: the wicked warriors and the virtuous warriors.
There are eight *vālukā* spirits who consume flesh and possess meager merit; their bodies are like sand and dust.
There are nine *yakṣa* spirits who possess great supernatural powers.
The ten *rākṣasa* spirits are translated as "extremely difficult to examine.
The Sūtra states:
"Great King, in your kingdom there will arise many bandits."
The commentary states:
Fourth, the explanation of the difficulties regarding that which is protected.
This section is divided into three parts:

First, the difficulties regarding ghosts and the like are clarified; next, the difficulties regarding the three calamities are clarified; and finally, from "All Invitations and Difficulties" onwards, the refutations are addressed and protection is distinguished.
This is the first [section].

Briefly, there are eight calamities: first, the disturbance of ghosts; second, the disturbance of the populace; third, rebels coming to plunder the state; fourth, the loss of life among the common people; fifth, disputes between ruler and minister; sixth, strange anomalies in heaven and earth; seventh, the constellations losing their proper courses; eighth, the sun and moon losing their proper courses—during which many rebellions arise.
Such difficulties as these cannot be recounted in full.

Regarding the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, in the "Moon Treasury" section (*Candragarbha-parivarta*), within the "Chapter on the Gathering of the Mansions," states: "There are seven mansions in each direction; thus, there are twenty-eight mansions in the four directions combined."
The seven lunar mansions of the eastern quarter are Jiao (Horn), Kang (Neck), Di (Base), Fang (Room), Xin (Heart), Wei (Tail), and Ji (Winnowing Basket).
The seven lunar mansions of the southern quarter are Jing (Well), Gui (Ghost), Liu (Willow), Xing (Star), Zhang (Spread), Yi (Wing), and Zhen (Chariot).
The seven lunar mansions of the western quarter are Kui, Wei, Mao, Bi, Zi, and Shen.
The seven lunar mansions of the northern quarter are Dou, Niu, Ni, Xu, Wei, Shi, and Bi.
Furthermore, the tenth fascicle of the *Candragarbha-parivarta* differs slightly from the above; fearing it would be too prolix, I shall not describe it here.
The Sūtra says:
"O Great King... up to all manner of difficulties."
The commentary states:
Second, the calamities of fire, water, and wind.
The Sūtra says:
One should also lecture on this sutra; the ritual application is as described above. (Alternatively, some versions read "lecture and recite this sutra.
The commentary states:
Third, according to the above, one protects the Dharma.

Sūtra: "Great King, not only does he protect the country... up to "...the application of the Dharma as explained above. An alternative version states: "...or reciting and reading this sūtra. Commentary:
Second, the clarification of the protection of the Dharma.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the application of the aforementioned method of protecting the Dharma, which may be understood from the text itself.
Question:
While it may be possible for wealthy and noble guests to attend a lecture, how can those who are poor and lowly achieve this?
According to the various difficulties mentioned below, such obstacles ought to exist.
If one follows this objection, then lecturing and reciting this sutra should be considered the correct practice.
The Sutra says:
"Great King, you protect not only merit, but also protect against various calamities."
The commentary states:
Third, the clarification of escaping all calamities.
There are three major categories:
First the heading, next the explanation, and finally the application.
This is the heading.
The Sūtra says:
"If diseases, calamities, and hardships arise—all manner of immeasurable sufferings and difficulties.
Commentary: This is the second section, providing a detailed explanation of various difficulties.

This refers to the hardships of retribution such as illness and the like, or shackles and the like; or the hardships of the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, the eight difficulties, and the karma of the six realms—all such immeasurable hardships of karmic fruition.
Regarding the "four grave offenses," these are the transgressions of sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and false speech.
Question:
By reciting and studying this sutra, can one protect against the karma of these four grave offenses?
If one is able to guard [the precepts], it should not constitute a loss of the precepts;
yet if the precepts have already been lost, how could one be able to guard them?
The explanation says:
The various schools differ.
According to the Hīnayāna, there are two distinct positions,
as described by three masters in the fifteenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
First, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the prātimokṣa vows are relinquished due to five conditions.

Their verse states: "The prātimokṣa discipline is relinquished by the abandonment [of the object], by death, by the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs, by the severance of the roots of virtue, and by the end of the night."
When one commits a fundamental pārājika offense, one does not forfeit the monastic precepts.
The reason for this is that it is not the case that by committing a single part, the entirety of the discipline (vinaya) must be universally forfeited.
Nevertheless, there are two names: namely, one who upholds the precepts and one who violates them.
It is like a wealthy person who, when owing a debt to another, is called both a rich man and a debtor.

If, regarding what was violated, one confesses and eliminates the transgression, they are said to possess *śīla* (virtuous conduct) and are no longer called a violator of the precepts; this is like having repaid the debt, whereby one is simply called a rich man.

Second, the Sautrāntika masters state that there are six conditions for relinquishing the *leśa* (minor rules) and the Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa vows: namely, the aforementioned five, with the addition of committing a grave offense (*pārājika*).

Third, the Dharmaguptaka masters state that there are seven conditions for relinquishing the Prātimokṣa vows: namely, the aforementioned six, with the addition of the disappearance of the True Dharma (*saddharma-antardhāna*).
The Sautrāntika challenges the Sarvāstivāda:

"If that is so, for what reason did the Blessed One say that one who has committed the four *pārājika* offenses is no longer called a bhikṣu, no longer called a śramaṇa, and is not a son of the Śākya; that he has destroyed the nature of a bhikṣu, harmed the nature of a śramaṇa, and being fallen and ruined, is designated by the name 'defeated' (*parājita*)?"
The Sarvāstivādins reply: This was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) regarding the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) of a bhikṣu.
At the time when the True Dharma perishes, one does not newly acquire [the status], nor does one abandon the precepts previously received.
The details are as explained there.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, the various teachings differ.
If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is stated that although one may commit a grave offense and lose the precepts, this does not constitute a failure to protect the Dharma.
The fortieth [chapter] states: "Briefly, there are two conditions by which one abandons the bodhisattva’s vow of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*):

first, the abandonment of the great aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; second, the commission of an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) through the manifestation of superior fetters (*paryavasthāna*)."

Although these bodhisattvas may change their bodies and be born everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they do not abandon the pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) of a bodhisattva.

Because these bodhisattvas do not forsake their great vow for unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*), they neither manifest the coarse fetters (*paryavasthāna*) nor commit any defeat (*pārājika*) offenses.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on the Treasury of Abhidharma), Chapter 53, states: "Question:
How many causes and conditions are there by which a bhikṣu’s discipline, once received, is subsequently relinquished?
Answer:"

The bhikṣu vows are relinquished through one of the following: by abandoning the precepts one has undertaken; by committing a root offense; by the disappearance of one's gender or the emergence of both genders; by severing the roots of virtue; or by discarding the homogeneous life-constituent (nikāya-sabhāga).
"If the True Dharma is destroyed and the True Dharma has vanished, although there is no new reception of the bhikṣu vows, it should be known that what was previously received is not lost.

According to the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*, it says: "If śrāvakas violate the Three Refuges and the five precepts, the eight precepts, the bhikṣu precepts, the bhikṣuṇī precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, the śrāmaṇerī precepts, the śikṣamāṇā precepts, and various codes of conduct—due to folly, unwholesomeness, and an evil and perverse mind—they frequently transgress these various precepts and codes of conduct."

If you wish to eliminate [faults] so that no further afflictions remain, and to once again become a bhikṣu endowed with the dharmas of a śramaṇa, you should diligently cultivate and study the Vaipulya sūtras, contemplate the ultimate truth of the profound dharma of emptiness, and cause this wisdom of emptiness to be in accord with the mind.
It should be known that for such a person, in every moment of thought, all defilements and sins are forever exhausted without remainder.
This is called being endowed with all the dharmas and precepts of a śramaṇa, and endowed with all dignified deportment.
Based on the Vaipulya sūtras and the text of this sūtra, it is also possible for one to be reborn [in the higher realms].

Thus, the first fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva violates any one of the twenty-four precepts, the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, the precepts of a śikṣamāṇā or śrāmaṇerikā, the bhikṣu precepts, or the bhikṣuṇī precepts—one should, with a single-minded resolve, repent of such violations."
It is impossible for one not to be reborn [in the Pure Land], except in the case of a lack of sincere resolve;
it is likewise impossible for one who has committed the five heinous crimes and suffers from white leprosy on the body for that condition not to be cured and eliminated.

Furthermore, the fourth [section] states: "If there is a bhikṣu who has violated the four grave prohibitions, he should with a sincere mind recollect this dhāraṇī sūtra and chant it one thousand four hundred times."
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand four hundred times, one should then perform repentance. Requesting a bhikṣu to serve as a witness, one confesses one's own transgressions before the image.
Proceeding in this manner for eighty-seven days of diligent repentance, it is impossible that these roots of the precepts would not be restored.
If that person, having diligently performed repentance for eighty-seven days, were not to become firm in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a thing would be impossible.

If one relies on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, there is both relinquishment and non-relinquishment: it is called "relinquishment" because the power to receive [the teaching] has been lost, yet it is called "non-relinquishment" because the reception of the sūtra itself has not been lost; it is like a parched seed which, though possessing substance, lacks the power [to sprout].
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle thirty-one, states: "Good son!
In the sūtras I have made this declaration:

'If there is a bhikṣu who has committed the four pārājika offenses, he is no longer called a bhikṣu; he is called a "broken bhikṣu," one who has already lost his status as a bhikṣu, and can no longer produce the seeds of the sprouts of goodness.'"
It is, for example, like a scorched seed that does not produce fruit, or like a *tāla* tree whose crown is destroyed and thus bears no fruit; so it is with a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has said that once bhikṣus have committed a grave transgression, they lose their bhikṣu precepts."
"Good son! In a sutra, I have described four kinds of bhikṣus for the sake of Upānanda:
first, those who have ultimately reached the Path; second, those who delight in the Path; third, those who receive the Path; and fourth, those who defile the Path."
"One who commits the four grave offenses is one who defiles the Way.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata has said that even after a bhikṣu commits the four grave offenses, he does not lose his prohibitive precepts.'"
Regarding these various schools, one should formulate four propositions:
first, those who never relinquish [the precepts], such as the Sarvāstivādins;
second, those who invariably relinquish the precepts, such as the Sautrāntika school and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Third, both relinquishing and not relinquishing, as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and others;
fourth, neither relinquishing nor not relinquishing, as in the *Vaipulya Sūtras* and the *Samantabhadra-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra*, among others.
If one does not abandon [the offense] through confession, or abandons it without confessing, this constitutes the second and fourth cases.
Why is this so? Generally speaking, there are two types of fourfold propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
First is the distinct entity (*pṛthag-bhāva*), as in the *Vibhāṣā* and other texts, where the third and fourth [factors] are established as distinct dharmas within the sentence.
Second is the interrogative entity (*praśna-bhāva*), wherein the third and fourth [factors] negate and affirm a single dharma.
If understood through the gate of affirmative expression (*vidhi*), it constitutes the third alternative;
if understood through the gate of negative expression (*pratiṣedha*), it constitutes the fourth alternative.
It is by virtue of this that the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the Vaipulya teachings are both identical and distinct.
Now, based on the Vaipulya sūtras and the text of this scripture, the various meanings of the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes (pañcānantarya) are established.

Regarding the five heinous crimes, they are also termed "immediate karmas" (ānantarya-karma), namely: killing one's father, killing one's mother, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, killing an Arhat, and shedding the blood of a Buddha.
Question:
Can these five heinous acts (ānantarya-karma) be protected against?
If they can be protected against while still existing, would they not then be non-determinate karma?
If one cannot protect [the precepts], this text would be contradictory.
The explanation says:
the various schools differ in their tenets.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there is a fixed reception of karma and no such thing as "protecting the Dharma," as is fully detailed in various treatises.
This has been examined based on the Sautrāntika school.
Now, relying on the Mahāyāna, the various teachings differ.
If there are no superior conditions, one will be reborn in hell;
if there are superior conditions, both possibilities apply.
According to one interpretation based on the *Zaoxiang jing* (Sutra on Image Making), although retribution is received, it is slight.

Therefore, that sutra states: "By virtue of the conditions of creating an image, one briefly experiences the fruits of the three evil realms and emerges swiftly without suffering, like an arrow shot into a forest that passes through without stopping."
The *Contemplation of Immeasurable Life* states: "Even those who have committed the five heinous crimes shall be born in the Western Land.
Yet both versions of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* state that such persons are not permitted to be born there.
According to the twentieth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Holy Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-parivarta*), King Ajātaśatru gave rise to the bodhicitta and did not enter hell.
Therefore, that sutra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One praised King Ajātaśatru:
'Excellent, excellent!
If there is anyone who can resolve to attain bodhicitta, you should know that such a person adorns the great assembly of the Buddha.'"
"Great King!

In the past, you first resolved your mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before the Buddha Vipaśyin; from that time until my appearance in the world, during all that interval, you have never fallen into hell to undergo suffering."
"Great King, you should know that the bodhicitta yields such immeasurable fruits and rewards. Great King,
from this day forward, you should always diligently cultivate the bodhicitta."
Furthermore, the preceding text states: "Because King Ajātaśatru gave rise to the Great Mind, all his grave offenses were individually rendered slight.
It further states: "King Ajātaśatru said to Jīvaka:
'While I am not yet dead, I have already attained a celestial body; I have cast off a short life and obtained a long one.'"
The detailed exposition is as stated therein.

Regarding the "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 568, states: "O Heavenly King, you should know that a bodhisattva will never be born in a state of lack of leisure."

These bodhisattvas have no evil karma that leads to rebirth in the hells; they have no violation of the precepts that leads to rebirth among animals; and they have no envy that leads to rebirth as hungry ghosts. They do not give rise to wrong views and always encounter virtuous friends. Their faculties are unimpaired, making them vessels for the Buddha-dharma. They are not born in border regions, nor are they dull-witted or ignorant, nor do they fail to distinguish between good and evil.
